group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 65-year-old woman was seen this afternoon in the pre-operative optimization clinic seven days before a planned open right hepatectomy to remove two 3-cm colorectal metastases situated in segments V and VI; the hepatobiliary team expects a generous subcostal incision with extension across midline, intermittent Pringle maneuvers, approximately five hours of operative time, blood loss in the 800–1 000 mL range, cell-saver use, and immediate transfer to the surgical intensive-care unit for ventilator weaning, central venous pressure–guided fluid management, and close monitoring for post-resection liver insufficiency. She parked on the third level of the visitor garage, walked the quarter-mile indoor skyway to registration while carrying a small backpack, and conversed without stopping, noting that around the house she continues to climb a full flight of stairs several times daily, gardens by bending and kneeling for 20-minute stretches, and pushes a 35-pound lawn spreader across level ground without chest tightness, dizziness, or undue breathlessness. She has never experienced exertional or rest angina, has not undergone coronary catheterization, has no record of abnormal stress testing, and last month completed a health-club treadmill program advancing to 4 mph at a 10 % incline for nine minutes before terminating because of thigh fatigue rather than cardiorespiratory limitation. Her medical history includes stage 2 essential hypertension diagnosed in her forties, well controlled with amlodipine 10 mg each morning and lisinopril 20 mg nightly, hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime, and type 2 diabetes discovered during a life-insurance examination eight years ago; glycemic targets have been maintained with metformin 1 000 mg twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg every morning, and lifestyle modification, most recent hemoglobin A1c 7.1 % three weeks ago. She explicitly states she has never required any injectable glucose-lowering therapy. There is no personal history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid surgery, seizure, or chronic cognitive deficit. Hepatic records show she completed neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy with capecitabine and oxaliplatin six months prior, followed by a three-month washout to allow recovery of platelet count and improvement of mild transaminase elevation; repeat liver function tests obtained one hour before today’s visit reveal alanine aminotransferase 32 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 98 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. The same venous specimen demonstrated sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.95 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 38 mL/min/1.73 m²; she attributes her chronic kidney impairment to long-standing hypertension and chemotherapeutic exposure, and nephrology follow-up two months ago recommended careful peri-operative volume status control and avoidance of nephrotoxic agents. Complete blood count today shows hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 246 × 10⁹/L, and white blood cells 5.9 × 10⁹/L. She has never smoked, drinks a single glass of wine on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Past surgical history includes an uncomplicated laparoscopic left hemicolectomy two years ago for primary colon carcinoma and remote tonsillectomy in childhood; no anesthesia-related difficulties or postoperative pulmonary complications were recorded. Both parents lived into their late seventies; her mother succumbed to pancreatic cancer, and her father died of complications of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease—there are no premature coronary or cerebrovascular events among first-degree relatives. Review of systems today is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pedal edema, palpitations, syncope, claudication, abdominal distension, easy bruising, or recent weight loss. After five minutes seated, vital signs taken in the right arm measured blood pressure 132/72 mm Hg, regular pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air, and oral temperature 36.7 °C; height 168 cm, weight 81 kg, body-mass index 28.7 kg/m². She appeared comfortable and euvolemic with warm extremities. Neck examination showed flat jugular venous contours at 45°, carotid pulses were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was palpated in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line without displacement. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2, no gallop, rub, or murmur. Lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation bilaterally. Abdomen demonstrated a healed left paramedian laparoscopic port scar, mild right upper-quadrant tenderness to deep palpation without rebound, and no palpable masses; liver span was estimated at 12 cm by percussion. Extremities were free of edema with 2+ dorsalis pedis pulses. Neurologic screening showed full orientation, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength throughout, normal vibration sense, and a brisk toe-tap gait without imbalance. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displayed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 94 ms, axis 20°, and upright T waves, unchanged from a tracing one year earlier. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography revealed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Airway evaluation documented Mallampati class II view, 4-cm inter-incisor distance, 7-cm thyromental distance, and full neck extension, with dentition intact. The anesthesia plan includes balanced volatile general anesthesia with low central venous pressure technique during parenchymal transection, invasive arterial and central venous monitoring, avoidance of nephrotoxic contrast, goal-directed crystalloid limited to 1 mL/kg/h outside of hemostatic periods, point-of-care thromboelastography to guide transfusion, continuation of antihypertensives and statin on the morning of surgery, withholding metformin the day prior to mitigate lactic acidosis risk, and strict postoperative glucose surveillance every four hours with sliding-scale subcutaneous correction as needed. Sequential compression devices will be applied in the operating room, and subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin will begin the evening of postoperative day 1 once hemostasis is secured. After a detailed discussion covering potential bleeding, bile leak, renal deterioration, thromboembolism, pulmonary complications, and the possibility of prolonged intensive-care stay, the patient accurately repeated medication instructions, fasting guidelines, and early ambulation goals and expressed understanding of and readiness for definitive liver resection.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) awards one point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery: open hepatectomy is intraperitoneal surgery = 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: no documented history = 0.
- Heart failure: no history or clinical findings = 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA = 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: diabetes is treated with oral agents only; planned postoperative correction insulin does not count = 0.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: measured creatinine is 1.95 mg/dL, below the threshold despite reduced eGFR = 0.
Total: 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
